query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrCoNi-based high-entropy alloys, inducing a shift in local short‐range ordering from an L11-dominant (homogenized) state to an L12-favored state (via appropriate heat-treatment) enhances toughness retention by altering dislocation slip behavior to a more ductile regime.
generation.material_initial_state: A CrCoNi high-entropy alloy in its homogenized state exhibiting primarily L11-type short-range order.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat-treatment that promotes the formation of L12-ordered nanoclusters.
generation.conditions: Test at ambient and moderately elevated temperatures, within the typical operating range for demanding engineering applications, and using alloys with similar CrCoNi compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local short-range order (i.e., the proportion of L11 vs. L12 nanoclusters) which governs dislocation mobility.
generation.mechanism: The heat-treatment modifies the nanocluster ordering, favoring L12-type chemical ordering. This altered short-range order changes the way dislocations move—shifting from slip behavior associated with less efficient energy dissipation (L11) to a mode that better absorbs deformation energy and hinders crack propagation—thus retaining toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the homogenized baseline, heat-treated samples with increased L12 ordering will exhibit altered dislocation slip behavior (observable via microscopy) and correspondingly improved toughness retention.
generation.baseline: The homogenized CrCoNi alloy with dominant L11 short-range order, which shows comparatively lower toughness retention under load.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in CrCoNi-based and similar medium/high-entropy alloys where chemical short-range ordering is prominent; the effect may differ in alloys dominated by other mechanisms (e.g., those where edge dislocations govern strength, as in certain refractory HEAs).
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative correlation between the fraction of L12 ordering and the degree of toughness retention remains to be precisely determined, and the mechanism’s applicability outside the CrCoNi system is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrCoNi alloy samples: one set in the homogenized state (predominantly L11 ordering) and one subjected to a controlled heat-treatment intended to promote L12 ordering. Characterize the short-range order in each set via electron diffraction and atom probe tomography. Perform standardized fracture toughness and dislocation slip tests (using in-situ TEM or similar techniques) on both sets.
measurements: Quantification of L11 vs. L12 ordering via electron-diffraction/atom probe
Observation of dislocation slip behaviors using high-resolution TEM
Fracture toughness and crack propagation metrics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a significant shift in short-range order (i.e., an increase in L12 ordering) or if, despite the shift, there is no statistically significant improvement (or even a deterioration) in toughness retention and dislocation behavior compared to the homogenized baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Data-driven electron-diffraction approach reveals local short-range ordering in CrCoNi with ordering effects

Abstract: The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys
